La Gomera Giant Lizard Gallotia bravoana is a critically endangered lacertid endemic to the small island of La Gomera in the Canary archipelago. Recent field surveys focusing on reproductive ecology have provided detailed morphometric data for this species. The eggs, which are laid in a single clutch per year, have a recorded wet weight of approximately 6 grams [Ww0 = approximately 6 grams]. When incubated under controlled thermal conditions matching the species' natural subterranean nest environment at 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the incubation period lasts about 60 days [ab = about 60 days], a duration typical for lacertids of comparable body size. Upon hatching, the neonates emerge with a snout-vent length averaging 5.5 centimeters [Lb = averaging 5.5 centimeters]. This relatively large size at hatching, compared to many other Gallotia species, may provide a survival advantage against invertebrate predators in the harsh, arid scrubland habitat of the island's steep barrancos.

As these juveniles grow and undergo their ontogenetic development, they progress through a distinct juvenile phase before reaching the size threshold associated with the onset of gonadal activity. Mark-recapture data indicate that individuals commence sexual maturation once they attain a snout-vent length of approximately 13.1 centimeters [Lp = approximately 13.1 centimeters]. Under a thermal regime reflecting mean field conditions of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the time elapsed from hatching to the achievement of puberty has been estimated at roughly 35 months after hatching [tp = roughly 35 months after hatching], a value derived from comparative studies on the closely related El Hierro Giant Lizard Gallotia simonyi. This relatively protracted developmental timeline is consistent with a slow life-history strategy typical of island endemics. During this period, the hatchlings weigh around 3.5 grams [Wwb = around 3.5 grams] at emergence, a modest mass that increases dramatically as the animals approach adulthood.

Significant sexual dimorphism in body size becomes apparent as the lizards approach their asymptotic dimensions. Adult males of Gallotia bravoana reach up to 19 centimeters [Li = up to 19 centimeters], whereas females are notably smaller, with a maximum recorded SVL of 15.5 centimeters [Li = 15.5 centimeters]. This size disparity is mirrored in their body masses; the ultimate wet weight of adult males can reach nearly 210.5 grams [Wwi = nearly 210.5 grams], while females achieve a peak body mass of approximately 159.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 159.2 grams]. Such pronounced sexual size dimorphism is a common feature within the genus Gallotia and is likely driven by sexual selection, as larger males may dominate access to basking sites and mates in the limited available habitat. The dimorphism also influences differential resource utilization between the sexes.

Reproductive output in this species is relatively constrained, with females producing a single clutch of eggs per year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs per year], a low annual frequency that reflects the energetic limitations of a large-bodied reptile living in a resource-poor environment. Each clutch typically contains approximately 7 eggs [N_R_i = Each clutch typically contains approximately 7 eggs], and the combination of this clutch size with a single annual clutch yields a modest annual reproductive output of about 7 eggs per year. These reproductive parameters place Gallotia bravoana at the slow extreme of the life-history continuum among lacertids. The energetic investment in each egg is substantial, as evidenced by the wet weight of individual eggs, which represents a significant proportion of the female's own body mass.

Longevity data for this species, again extrapolated from observations on Gallotia simonyi under controlled conditions at a constant 24 °C [T = 24 °C], suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 133 months [am = approximately 133 months], approaching 11 years, and is characteristic of large-bodied island lizards that face few native mammalian predators and have evolved a slow pace of life. The combination of delayed maturation taking about 35 months after hatching [tp = about 35 months after hatching], low annual reproductive output of just one clutch per year, and high adult survival underscores a conservative life-history strategy making the population highly sensitive to adult mortality, as even a small increase in predation pressure could drive the species toward local extinction at a temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. Such traits make the species particularly vulnerable to extinction from introduced predators or habitat alteration, as the population's intrinsic rate of increase is very low. Conservation efforts for this critically endangered lacertid must therefore prioritize the protection of adult individuals and their breeding microhabitats.
